messages.content: Could you retrieve the current weather data for New York, specifically focusing on the temperature?.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.reasoning:
We need to call the function requests_get with appropriate parameters. For New York, latitude ~40.7128, longitude -74.0060. We want temperature. The Open-Meteo API endpoint likely is something like "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast". We need to specify params: latitude, longitude, maybe "current_weather=true" to get current weather. The function signature includes params: {latitude?, longitude?, elevation?}. But we also need to pass other query parameters like "current_weather=true". However the function signature only allows latitude, longitude, elevation. It doesn't allow arbitrary query parameters. That might be a limitation. But maybe we can include them in the URL? The function signature has "params" only for those three fields. So we cannot pass "current_weather=true". But maybe the API defaults to returning current weather? Not sure. The Open-Meteo API requires "current_weather=true" to get current weather. Without it, it returns forecast. But we can still get temperature from forecast? The forecast includes hourly temperatures. But we want current temperature. We could use "hourly=temperature_2m" and then pick the latest hour. But the function signature doesn't allow specifying "hourly". So we can't.

Thus we might need to construct the URL with query parameters manually. The function signature has "url" and "params" but params only includes latitude, longitude, elevation. But we can embed other query parameters in the URL itself. For example: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=40.7128&longitude=-74.0060&current_weather=true". Then we don't need to use params. But the function signature expects "params" object. But we can set params empty. The URL already contains query parameters. That should work.

So we call requests_get with url: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=40.7128&longitude=-74.0060&current_weather=true". No headers needed. Use default headers. No params. Let's do that.
